plan.chapterName: OpenStax Precalculus 2e, chapter 8: Further Applications of Trigonometry
plan.contextChunk: This figure shows two rose curves plotted on separate polar grids, set side by side and labeled (a) and (b) beneath. Each grid is built from dotted concentric circles crossed by dotted radial spokes, with solid horizontal and vertical axes arrowed at all four ends. Panel (a) holds a teal curve of eight identical petals, all springing from the origin at equal angular intervals so that four lie along the axes and four along the diagonals between them; its caption reads r = acos(n theta), n even. Panel (b) holds a curve in the same teal weight but with only three petals, one pointing straight down along the negative vertical axis and the other two angled up to the left and up to the right, spaced a third of a turn apart; its caption reads r = asin(n theta), n odd. Every petal reaches out to roughly the same radius, so each curve fills a circular envelope. Setting the panels side by side isolates the parity of n as the only thing governing the count: an even n produces 2n petals while an odd n produces just n, and the eight-petal and three-petal drawings are the two cases of that rule.

interactionPlan.concept: For a rose curve r = a·cos(nθ) or r = a·sin(nθ), the integer n sets the petal count by its parity (odd n → n petals, even n → 2n petals), the sine/cosine choice sets the orientation, and a sets only the petal length.
elements: Single large polar grid centered in the panel (replacing the side-by-side pair, with a compare mode that shows both cases)
Dotted concentric circles at equal radial increments (unit rings) forming the polar grid
Dotted radial spokes every 30° (or π/6) crossing the rings
Solid horizontal axis with arrowheads at both ends (polar axis, θ = 0 to the right)
Solid vertical axis with arrowheads at both ends (θ = π/2 up)
Teal rose curve drawn with a thick stroke, all petals emanating from the origin
Faint gray outer circle of radius a marking the envelope every petal reaches
Formula caption rendered live beneath the grid, e.g. 'r = a cos(nθ)' with current a and n substituted
Petal-count readout badge, e.g. 'n = 4 (even) → 2n = 8 petals'
Small moving dot at the current (r, θ) point when the curve is being traced, with a dashed radius segment from origin to the dot
Angle readout for the traced θ in radians and degrees
Shaded/highlighted first petal (θ from 0 to π/n) to show the generating interval
Reference panel labels '(a) n even — 2n petals' and '(b) n odd — n petals' in compare mode
Legend: teal = current rose, gray dotted = polar grid, gray circle = radius a

interactions.label: Petal parameter n
interactions.teaches: Stepping n one integer at a time makes the alternation obvious: petal count jumps 1, 4, 3, 8, 5, 12, 7, 16 — odd n gives n petals, even n gives 2n.

interactions.label: Form
interactions.teaches: Switching cos ↔ sin rotates the whole rose by π/(2n) — orientation changes, petal count does not, so parity and orientation are independent facts.

interactions.label: Amplitude a
interactions.teaches: a is the maximum radius: every petal stretches or shrinks together and the number of petals never changes, so a controls size alone.

interactions.label: Trace θ up to
interactions.teaches: Sweeping θ from 0 to 2π and beyond shows WHY parity matters: for odd n the second half of the sweep retraces petals already drawn (negative r lands on the same rays), while for even n it draws a fresh set in between.

interactions.label: Edit the rose
interactions.teaches: Typing your own coefficient and frequency confirms the rule generalizes: any a and integer n you choose obeys the same petal-count and orientation behavior, and non-integer n breaks the closed rose entirely.

demo_steps.title: Start with one petal
demo_steps.narration: With n = 1 the curve r = a cos(θ) is a single circular petal along the polar axis. This is the simplest rose and the baseline for counting.

demo_steps.title: Odd n: three petals
demo_steps.narration: Set n = 3 and three petals appear, not six. Slide the trace back and watch: after θ = π the curve simply retraces the same three petals, because negative r flips the point onto a ray already used.

demo_steps.title: Even n: petal count doubles
demo_steps.narration: Now n = 4 — the figure from panel (a). Eight petals fill the circle: four along the axes and four on the diagonals. Nothing is retraced, so the count is 2n.

demo_steps.title: Sine rotates, it does not recount
demo_steps.narration: Toggle to the sine form with n = 3 to reproduce panel (b): still three petals, but the rose has rotated by π/(2n) so one petal points straight down. Orientation and parity are separate ideas.

demo_steps.title: a changes size only
demo_steps.narration: Drag the amplitude down and every petal shortens to the new maximum radius a, all together. The three petals stay three petals — a scales the rose, n counts it.

demo_steps.title: Test the rule yourself
demo_steps.narration: Step to a large even n, then type your own r(θ) in the equation box. Predict the petal count before the graph redraws — and try a non-integer n to see the rose fail to close.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: Odd n gives n petals only because the second half of the θ-sweep retraces the first half; even n has nothing to retrace, so the petals double to 2n — the parity rule is a statement about retracing, not a fact to memorize.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Center a polar grid on a white background: roughly five dotted gray concentric circles and twelve dotted radial spokes at 30° intervals, with solid black horizontal and vertical axes carrying arrowheads at all four ends. Draw the rose in a thick teal stroke (matching the original's blue-teal, ~#1B87A8), every petal springing from the origin and reaching the same outer radius so the curve fills a circular envelope; a faint gray circle of radius a marks that envelope. Default view reproduces panel (a): eight equal petals from r = a cos(4θ), four on the axes and four on the diagonals. The sine/odd case reproduces panel (b): three petals, one pointing straight down, the other two up-left and up-right, 120° apart. Below the grid render the live formula in italic serif math style, 'r = a cos(nθ)' or 'r = a sin(nθ)', with the current numeric a and n, plus a small badge stating the parity and resulting petal count. While tracing, show a filled teal dot at the current point with a dashed radius to the origin and a θ readout; draw the already-traced arc solid teal and the untraced remainder as a faint teal ghost so retracing versus new-petal drawing is visually distinguishable. A compare mode may place the even and odd cases side by side with '(a)' and '(b)' captions underneath, matching the original layout.

authoredContext:
The formulas that generate the graph of a rose curve are given by r=acosnθ and r=asinnθ where a≠0. If n is even, the curve has 2n petals. If n is odd, the curve has n petals. See the figure.

Graph of two rose curves side by side. (A) is r=acos(ntheta), where n is even. Eight petals extending from origin, equally spaced. (B) is r=asin(ntheta) where n is odd. Three petals extending from the origin, equally spaced.

discrepancies: Captions substitute the numeric amplitude ('r = 4 cos(4θ), n even') where the source uses the symbolic italic 'a' ('r = a cos(nθ), n even'), so the general form that the textbook figure is illustrating is lost in the default view.
A solid light-gray envelope circle r = a is drawn in each panel; no such circle exists in the source (only the dotted polar rings and diagonals).
Extra sub-captions '8 petals' / '3 petals' are added under each panel; not present in the original.
The two panels are pushed to the upper-left with a large empty band of whitespace below the (a)/(b) tags, so the composition is less balanced/less tightly cropped than the source.
Petals in the generated roses are slightly narrower/less rounded than the source lobes, and the curve stroke is a bit thinner relative to panel size.
evaluation.notes: Default two-panel compare view is clearly recognizable as the source rose-curve figure (correct petal counts, teal curves, dotted polar grid, arrowed axes), with an unusually rich and well-wired set of interactions (n slider, sin/cos toggle, amplitude, θ-sweep with animation, petal highlight, custom r(θ), step player); main weaknesses are the numeric rather than symbolic captions, an added envelope circle and petal-count sub-labels, and unused whitespace below the panels.
action_items: In compare (default) mode, render the captions symbolically as 'r = a cos(nθ), n even' and 'r = a sin(nθ), n odd' (reserve the numeric live formula for the single-panel/explore mode).

Suppress the gray envelope circle and the '8 petals'/'3 petals' sub-labels in the default compare view (or make them appear only on hover/explore) so step-0 is a drop-in replacement for the static figure.
Rebalance the layout: enlarge the two panels and reduce the empty vertical band under the (a)/(b) tags so the composition matches the source crop.
Thicken the rose stroke slightly and widen the petal rendering to better match the rounded lobes of the source curve.

feedback.rationale: The concept and interaction structure are correct; remaining issues are concrete rendering fixes (symbolic captions, removing added envelope circle and sub-labels, layout balance, stroke weight).

Angle readout for the traced θ in radians and degrees
Shaded/highlighted first petal (θ from 0 to π/n) to show the generating interval
Reference panel labels '(a) n even — 2n petals' and '(b) n odd — n petals' in compare mode
Legend: teal = current rose, gray dotted = polar grid, gray circle = radius a

interactions.label: Petal parameter n
interactions.teaches: Stepping n one integer at a time makes the alternation obvious: petal count jumps 1, 4, 3, 8, 5, 12, 7, 16 — odd n gives n petals, even n gives 2n.

interactions.label: Form
interactions.teaches: Switching cos ↔ sin rotates the whole rose by π/(2n) — orientation changes, petal count does not, so parity and orientation are independent facts.

interactions.label: Amplitude a
interactions.teaches: a is the maximum radius: every petal stretches or shrinks together and the number of petals never changes, so a controls size alone.

interactions.label: Trace θ up to
interactions.teaches: Sweeping θ from 0 to 2π and beyond shows WHY parity matters: for odd n the second half of the sweep retraces petals already drawn (negative r lands on the same rays), while for even n it draws a fresh set in between.

interactions.label: Edit the rose
interactions.teaches: Typing your own coefficient and frequency confirms the rule generalizes: any a and integer n you choose obeys the same petal-count and orientation behavior, and non-integer n breaks the closed rose entirely.

demo_steps.title: Start with one petal
demo_steps.narration: With n = 1 the curve r = a cos(θ) is a single circular petal along the polar axis. This is the simplest rose and the baseline for counting.

demo_steps.title: Odd n: three petals
demo_steps.narration: Set n = 3 and three petals appear, not six. Slide the trace back and watch: after θ = π the curve simply retraces the same three petals, because negative r flips the point onto a ray already used.

demo_steps.title: Even n: petal count doubles
demo_steps.narration: Now n = 4 — the figure from panel (a). Eight petals fill the circle: four along the axes and four on the diagonals. Nothing is retraced, so the count is 2n.

demo_steps.title: Sine rotates, it does not recount
demo_steps.narration: Toggle to the sine form with n = 3 to reproduce panel (b): still three petals, but the rose has rotated by π/(2n) so one petal points straight down. Orientation and parity are separate ideas.

demo_steps.title: a changes size only
demo_steps.narration: Drag the amplitude down and every petal shortens to the new maximum radius a, all together. The three petals stay three petals — a scales the rose, n counts it.

demo_steps.title: Test the rule yourself
demo_steps.narration: Step to a large even n, then type your own r(θ) in the equation box. Predict the petal count before the graph redraws — and try a non-integer n to see the rose fail to close.

plan.keyInsight: Odd n gives n petals only because the second half of the θ-sweep retraces the first half; even n has nothing to retrace, so the petals double to 2n — the parity rule is a statement about retracing, not a fact to memorize.
plan.reconstructionNotes: Center a polar grid on a white background: roughly five dotted gray concentric circles and twelve dotted radial spokes at 30° intervals, with solid black horizontal and vertical axes carrying arrowheads at all four ends. Draw the rose in a thick teal stroke (matching the original's blue-teal, ~#1B87A8), every petal springing from the origin and reaching the same outer radius so the curve fills a circular envelope; a faint gray circle of radius a marks that envelope. Default view reproduces panel (a): eight equal petals from r = a cos(4θ), four on the axes and four on the diagonals. The sine/odd case reproduces panel (b): three petals, one pointing straight down, the other two up-left and up-right, 120° apart. Below the grid render the live formula in italic serif math style, 'r = a cos(nθ)' or 'r = a sin(nθ)', with the current numeric a and n, plus a small badge stating the parity and resulting petal count. While tracing, show a filled teal dot at the current point with a dashed radius to the origin and a θ readout; draw the already-traced arc solid teal and the untraced remainder as a faint teal ghost so retracing versus new-petal drawing is visually distinguishable. A compare mode may place the even and odd cases side by side with '(a)' and '(b)' captions underneath, matching the original layout.

discrepancies: Rose scale relative to the polar grid: in the source the petal tips reach the outermost dotted ring, whereas the default a = 4 of 5 grid units leaves the petals ending inside the second-outermost ring in both panels.
Extra sub-captions '(n = 4) → 8 petals' / '(n = 3) → 3 petals' appear under each formula; these are not in the source and add a third text line beneath each panel.
Petal stroke weight is slightly thinner and petals slightly narrower than the source's rather full, rounded lobes, giving a somewhat sparser look.
Grid ray density: source shows diagonal dotted lines that extend past the outer ring and slightly heavier dotting; the generated rays stop exactly at the outer ring.
evaluation.notes: Very close reproduction of the two-panel rose-curve figure (correct 8-petal cos and correctly oriented 3-petal sin roses, dotted polar grid, arrowed axes, italic serif captions) backed by a rich, genuinely functional control set (n slider, sine toggle, amplitude, θ-sweep with animation, petal shading, compare toggle, custom r(θ), 6-step narrated demo); main weaknesses are a rose that under-fills the grid at default a, added count sub-captions not in the source, and a step narration inviting non-integer n that the integer-only slider cannot produce.
action_items: Set the default amplitude so petal tips touch the outermost dotted ring (e.g. a = 5 with 5 rings) so panel (a)/(b) match the source proportions.

Hide or de-emphasize the '(n = …) → N petals' sub-captions in the default overview state so the step-0 view reads as a drop-in replacement for the static figure (reveal them only once the user moves a control).
Thicken the rose stroke slightly and widen the petals marginally to match the fuller lobes of the source line art.
Either allow fractional n (step 0.5) or reword the final step's 'try a non-integer n' instruction to point explicitly at the custom r(θ) box.
